flags.heading: A Church Needing Coordinated Missions
flags.text: By the early seventeenth century, Catholic missionary activity had spread across the Americas, Asia, and Africa through a patchwork of religious orders, royal patronage arrangements, and local episcopal initiative, often working with little central coordination and, at times, in open competition or conflict with one another over jurisdiction and method — a situation that left Rome itself with limited direct oversight of a missionary enterprise it nonetheless bore ultimate responsibility for.

flags.heading: Founded by Gregory XV
flags.text: Pope Gregory XV addressed this fragmentation by establishing, through the bull Inscrutabili Divinae of 22 June 1622, the Sacred Congregation for the Propagation of the Faith — Propaganda Fide — a permanent Roman office charged with the coordination, training, and direct oversight of the Church's worldwide missionary work, freed as far as possible from the competing claims of individual religious orders and European royal patronage systems (the padroado and patronato arrangements) that had often placed missionary appointments under secular rather than papal control.

flags.heading: Founded by Gregory XV
flags.text: The new congregation's very independence from royal patronage systems made it, from the outset, a source of real friction with Catholic monarchies accustomed to controlling ecclesiastical appointments within their own colonial territories, a tension that would recur throughout the congregation's history wherever missionary work intersected with European colonial administration.

flags.heading: An Urban College for Missionaries
flags.text: Gregory's successor, Pope Urban VIII, extended the new congregation's reach in 1627 by founding the Urban College, a seminary in Rome dedicated specifically to training missionary priests, including candidates drawn directly from mission territories themselves — an early and genuinely significant effort to cultivate native clergy rather than relying exclusively on European missionaries sent outward from Rome.

flags.heading: Rome's Direct Hand in the Missions
flags.text: Propaganda Fide's establishment marked a deliberate shift toward centralized papal direction of missionary strategy: the new congregation reviewed and approved missionary appointments, arbitrated jurisdictional disputes among competing religious orders working the same territory, and issued guidance on questions of inculturation and missionary method that would shape debates — some of them, such as the Chinese Rites controversy, genuinely contentious — for generations afterward.

flags.heading: Legacy
flags.text: Renamed the Congregation for the Evangelization of Peoples in 1988 under Pope John Paul II's reorganization of the Roman Curia, the office founded in 1622 remains, four centuries later, the central Vatican body responsible for the Church's missionary activity across those regions still formally designated as mission territory — a lasting institutional answer to the coordination problem Gregory XV first set out to solve, and a structure that has outlasted the colonial patronage systems it was originally created, in part, to counterbalance.

flags.heading: A Society Under Growing Attack
flags.text: By the mid-eighteenth century, the Society of Jesus — wealthy, influential, and deeply embedded in the education, confessional counsel, and missionary work of Catholic Europe and its colonies — had accumulated powerful enemies among Enlightenment critics of Church influence, Jansenist rivals within the Church itself, and above all the absolutist monarchs of Catholic Europe, who increasingly resented the Society's independence from royal control and its direct obedience to the pope.

flags.heading: Expelled Kingdom by Kingdom
flags.text: Beginning with Portugal in 1759, followed by France in 1764 and Spain and its vast American empire in 1767, one Catholic monarchy after another expelled the Jesuits from its territories, seizing their considerable property and confiscating their schools and missions, often on fabricated or exaggerated charges of conspiracy and disloyalty; the Bourbon courts of Spain, France, and Naples then jointly pressed the papacy itself to dissolve the order entirely.

flags.heading: Clement XIV's Decision
flags.text: Under sustained and unrelenting political pressure from the Bourbon monarchies, Pope Clement XIV issued the brief Dominus ac Redemptor on 21 July 1773, suppressing the Society of Jesus throughout the Catholic world — dissolving its governing structure, releasing its members from their Jesuit vows, and placing its considerable property and institutions under local episcopal control.

flags.heading: Clement XIV's Decision
flags.text: The pope's own private correspondence suggests he acted less from conviction that the Society had genuinely erred than from a judgment that its continued existence threatened a far more damaging rupture with the Bourbon courts.

flags.heading: Survival Under a Sympathetic Empress
flags.text: The suppression was never fully enforced everywhere: Catherine the Great of Russia, whose territory included formerly Polish lands with an active Jesuit presence, declined to promulgate the papal brief within her own dominions, allowing a small remnant of the Society to continue functioning legally in Russian territory throughout the decades of formal suppression elsewhere — an unlikely refuge for a Catholic religious order preserved by the deliberate choice of an Orthodox empress.

flags.heading: Legacy
flags.text: The Society of Jesus remained suppressed for over four decades, its former members scattered into diocesan ministry or other communities, until Pope Pius VII, restored to Rome after the fall of Napoleon, formally revived the order worldwide in 1814 through the bull Sollicitudo Omnium Ecclesiarum — drawing in part on the very Russian remnant that had quietly kept the Jesuit tradition of formation and governance alive throughout the long years of suppression elsewhere, and allowing the Society to resume, within a generation, much of the missionary and educational work for which it had once been suppressed.

flags.heading: A Long-Held Belief
flags.text: The conviction that the Blessed Virgin Mary was preserved free from original sin from the very moment of her conception had deep roots in the Church's liturgical and popular devotion, with feasts of the Conception of Mary celebrated in East and West for centuries.

flags.heading: Growing Consensus
flags.text: By the seventeenth century, popes such as Alexander VII had already affirmed the doctrine as among the truths revealed by God, even without a formal dogmatic definition, and devotion to the Immaculate Conception flourished widely across the Catholic world, marked by countless churches, confraternities, and works of art dedicated under this title.

flags.heading: Pius IX's Definition
flags.text:
On 8 December 1854, surrounded by a great assembly of cardinals and bishops in St. Peter's Basilica, Pope Pius IX promulgated the apostolic constitution Ineffabilis Deus, solemnly defining that the Blessed Virgin Mary
"in the first instance of her conception, by a singular privilege and grace granted by God, in view of the merits of Jesus Christ, the Saviour of the human race, was preserved exempt from all stain of original sin."

flags.heading: What the Dogma Teaches
flags.text: The definition applies specifically to the moment of the infusion of Mary's soul into her body in her mother's womb, not to the manner of her parents' conception, teaching that she alone among human beings, by a unique grace flowing from the future merits of Christ's redemption, never bore the stain of original sin inherited by the rest of humanity from Adam.

flags.heading: Confirmation at Lourdes
flags.text: Catholics have long seen a striking confirmation of the newly defined dogma in the apparitions at Lourdes barely four years later, in 1858, when the visionary St. Bernadette Soubirous reported that the lady who appeared to her identified herself, in the local Occitan dialect, with words rendered in French as 'Que soy era Immaculada Councepciou' — 'I am the Immaculate Conception,' a title the young, unlettered peasant girl could not plausibly have invented herself.

flags.heading: Legacy
flags.text: Ineffabilis Deus stands as one of the two occasions on which a pope has exercised the extraordinary charism of infallibility to define a Marian dogma, the other being the 1950 definition of the Assumption.

flags.heading: Legacy
flags.text: The definition further fueled Marian devotion across the Catholic world in the century that followed and remains a touchstone for Catholic teaching on grace, redemption, and Mary's unique role in salvation history.

flags.heading: A Shrinking Temporal Domain
flags.text: The nineteenth-century movement for Italian unification (the Risorgimento), led by figures such as Camillo Cavour and Giuseppe Garibaldi under King Victor Emmanuel II of Piedmont-Sardinia, viewed papal temporal rule as the chief obstacle to a unified Italian nation.

flags.heading: Losses Under Pius IX
flags.text: Piedmontese forces annexed most of the Papal States' outlying provinces by 1860, defeating papal troops at Castelfidardo, and reduced Pope Pius IX's temporal domain to Rome and its immediate surroundings, protected for a time only by a French garrison stationed there at Napoleon III's order.

flags.heading: The Capture of Rome
flags.text: On 20 September 1870, Italian artillery breached the ancient walls near the Porta Pia, and Italian troops occupied the city after only token resistance from the small papal garrison, formally ending more than a millennium of papal temporal sovereignty.

flags.heading: 'A Prisoner of the Vatican'
flags.text: Pius IX refused to recognize the seizure or to accept the Italian government's unilateral Law of Guarantees, which offered him certain privileges and an annual indemnity in exchange for accepting the loss of Rome.

flags.heading: 'A Prisoner of the Vatican'
flags.text: Instead, he confined himself to the Vatican for the rest of his pontificate, declaring himself a 'prisoner of the Vatican' — a self-imposed status his successors Leo XIII, Pius X, Benedict XV, and Pius XI would maintain for nearly sixty years.

flags.heading: The Roman Question
flags.text: The resulting impasse, known as the Roman Question, poisoned relations between the Holy See and the Italian state for decades: popes forbade Catholic participation in Italian national politics (the non expedit), while the Vatican pressed unsuccessfully for international recognition of its independence and territorial claims.

flags.heading: Legacy
flags.text: The Roman Question remained unresolved until the Lateran Treaty of 1929, when Pope Pius XI and Mussolini's government finally settled the dispute, creating the sovereign Vatican City State in exchange for the papacy's formal recognition of the Kingdom of Italy.

flags.heading: Legacy
flags.text: The nearly six-decade standoff shaped the modern papacy's self-understanding as a spiritual rather than a great territorial power, a shift historians have called the definitive end of the medieval union of papal spiritual and temporal rule.

flags.heading: The Social Question
flags.text: By the late nineteenth century, the Industrial Revolution had transformed working life across Europe and America, concentrating vast wealth among factory owners while masses of laborers endured long hours, dangerous conditions, and meager wages, often uprooted from traditional rural communities into crowded industrial cities.

flags.heading: Leo XIII's Intervention
flags.text: Pope Leo XIII, drawing on the work of Catholic social thinkers such as Cardinal Gaspard Mermillod's Fribourg Union and bishops including Cardinal James Gibbons in America, issued the encyclical Rerum Novarum ('Of New Things') on 15 May 1891, subtitled 'On the Condition of Labor.'

flags.heading: A Middle Way
flags.text:
He insisted that a just wage must allow a working man to support himself and his family in reasonable comfort, writing that if a worker
"accept harder conditions because an employer or contractor will afford him no better, he is made the victim of force and injustice."

flags.heading: Rights and Duties on All Sides
flags.text: The encyclical laid out mutual obligations: the state's duty to protect workers' rights and promote the common good without absorbing all property into itself; employers' duty to pay fair wages and provide safe conditions; and workers' right to form associations and unions to defend their interests, a position that gave crucial Church encouragement to the nascent Catholic labor movement in many countries.

flags.heading: Immediate Reception
flags.text: The encyclical drew both praise and criticism: some economic liberals faulted its skepticism of unregulated markets, and some socialists, including the American economist Henry George, wrote extended public rebuttals defending broader property reforms.

flags.heading: Legacy
flags.text: Rerum Novarum is universally regarded as the founding document of modern Catholic social teaching, inaugurating a tradition of papal social encyclicals that continued through Pius XI's Quadragesimo Anno (1931, its fortieth anniversary), John XXIII's Mater et Magistra, John Paul II's Centesimus Annus (its centenary, 1991), and beyond, establishing principles of subsidiarity, solidarity, and the dignity of labor that remain central to Catholic engagement with economic life today.

flags.heading: A Young Priest in Madrid
flags.text: Josemaría Escrivá, born in Barbastro, Spain, in 1902, was ordained a priest in 1925 and moved to Madrid to pursue a doctorate in civil law, all the while sensing, as he later described it, an unclear but persistent call from God to some particular mission he could not yet identify.

flags.heading: The Foundational Vision
flags.text: On 2 October 1928, while making a retreat at a house of the Vincentian Fathers on the outskirts of Madrid, Escrivá experienced what he described as a divine illumination in which he 'saw' Opus Dei — a new path within the Church calling ordinary lay Christians, in every walk of life and profession, to seek holiness precisely through their everyday work and family responsibilities, rather than by leaving secular life for the cloister.

flags.heading: Founding Members and Early Growth
flags.text: In 1930, he understood that the message was intended for women as well, and by 1933 the first center, the DYA Academy offering law and architecture classes, opened in Madrid, blending professional formation with the spiritual message of Opus Dei.

flags.heading: Surviving the Spanish Civil War
flags.text: The Spanish Civil War beginning in 1936 brought severe anti-Catholic persecution, forcing Escrivá and members of Opus Dei in Republican-controlled areas into hiding or exile for their safety; the founder eventually crossed the Pyrenees via Andorra to reach Nationalist-held territory.

flags.heading: Official Recognition
flags.text: Decades later, in 1982, Pope John Paul II established Opus Dei as the Catholic Church's first personal prelature — a structure allowing it to operate across diocesan boundaries worldwide under its own prelate.

flags.heading: Legacy
flags.text: Opus Dei's core teaching — that ordinary work, faithfully and lovingly performed, can itself become a path to sanctity — has become one of the most influential expressions of the lay spirituality later emphasized by the Second Vatican Council's universal call to holiness, and the prelature today counts tens of thousands of members across the world.

flags.heading: Nearly Sixty Years Unresolved
flags.text: Since Italian troops seized Rome in 1870, ending papal temporal rule over the former Papal States, successive popes had refused to recognize the Kingdom of Italy's sovereignty over the city and had declined the unilateral Italian Law of Guarantees, considering themselves 'prisoners of the Vatican.'

flags.heading: Pius XI Seeks Reconciliation
flags.text: Upon his election in 1922, Pope Pius XI signaled his eagerness to resolve the impasse, and secret negotiations began in 1926 between Domenico Barone for the Italian government and Francesco Pacelli, brother of the future Pius XII, representing the Holy See.

flags.heading: Signing the Pacts
flags.text: On 11 February 1929, at the Lateran Palace in Rome, Cardinal Secretary of State Pietro Gasparri signed the agreements on behalf of Pius XI, and Prime Minister Benito Mussolini signed on behalf of King Victor Emmanuel III.

flags.heading: Signing the Pacts
flags.text: The Lateran Pacts consisted of three parts: a political treaty creating the sovereign Vatican City State; a financial convention compensating the Holy See for its lost territories; and a concordat regulating the position of the Catholic Church within Italian law and society.

flags.heading: Terms of the Settlement
flags.text: The treaty recognized the pope's full and exclusive sovereignty over the newly created Vatican City, a territory of just over 100 acres, in exchange for the Holy See's formal recognition of the Kingdom of Italy with Rome as its capital.

flags.heading: A Complicated Alliance
flags.text: The agreement was concluded with Mussolini's Fascist government, a fact that has drawn ongoing historical scrutiny and debate over the motives on each side — genuine ecclesial reconciliation for Pius XI, political legitimacy for Mussolini's regime.

flags.heading: Legacy
flags.text: The Lateran Treaty definitively resolved the Roman Question and remains, in modified form (renegotiated in 1984), the legal basis for Vatican City's status as the world's smallest sovereign state and the seat of the Holy See's independence from any other government.

flags.heading: Legacy
flags.text: It established the framework under which the papacy has operated ever since — as a spiritual authority backed by a minimal but fully sovereign territorial base, rather than the extensive temporal kingdom the popes once ruled.

flags.heading: An Ancient Belief, Long Held
flags.text: The conviction that the Blessed Virgin Mary, at the close of her earthly life, was assumed body and soul into heavenly glory reaches back to the earliest centuries of the Church's devotional life, commemorated liturgically in both East and West for well over a millennium before it was ever formally defined as dogma; the belief rests not on any explicit scriptural narrative of the event itself, since Scripture is silent on the end of Mary's earthly life, but on a constant and universal Christian tradition the Church came to recognize as an authentic part of the deposit of faith.

flags.heading: A Petition from the Whole Church
flags.text: In the years following the Second World War, Pope Pius XII received petitions from bishops, theologians, and ordinary faithful across the world requesting a formal dogmatic definition of the Assumption, a groundswell of devotion the pope took as significant evidence of what theologians call the sensus fidelium — the settled conviction of the whole body of believers regarding a truth of the faith, even one never previously defined with formal dogmatic precision.

flags.heading: A Petition from the Whole Church
flags.text: Pius XII had, in the years leading up to the definition, formally polled every bishop of the Catholic world on whether the doctrine was suitable for definition and whether the faithful desired it — a consultation that returned an overwhelming, near-unanimous affirmative response, giving the eventual definition an unusually broad and deliberately sought episcopal consensus behind it.

flags.heading: Munificentissimus Deus
flags.text:
On 1 November 1950, the Feast of All Saints, Pius XII promulgated the apostolic constitution Munificentissimus Deus, solemnly defining as a dogma to be held by the whole Church that the Blessed Virgin Mary,
"having completed the course of her earthly life, was assumed body and soul into heavenly glory."
The definition deliberately left open the disputed question of whether Mary actually experienced physical death before her assumption, a matter theologians continue to debate without the dogma itself resolving it either way.

flags.heading: A Fitting Completion
flags.text: The Church has traditionally understood the Assumption as a fitting culmination of Mary's unique role in salvation history: since she had borne in her own body the Author of Life, and had been preserved from sin from the first moment of her conception by the dogma Pius IX defined in 1854, it seemed fitting that she should not undergo the ordinary bodily corruption that awaits fallen humanity, but be taken instead, body and soul, into the glory her Son had already won.

flags.heading: Legacy
flags.text: Munificentissimus Deus stands as one of only two occasions, alongside the 1854 definition of the Immaculate Conception, on which a pope has exercised the extraordinary charism of papal infallibility to define a specifically Marian dogma — and, more broadly, remains among the very few instances in the whole history of the Church in which a pope has invoked the infallible teaching authority defined at the First Vatican Council to settle a matter of doctrine independent of a general council.

flags.heading: Legacy
flags.text: The dogma continues to shape Catholic Marian devotion and theology, offering, in the Church's own understanding, a promise held out to every believer of the bodily glorification that awaits all who are united to Christ.

flags.heading: A Year of Three Popes
flags.text: 1978 became known, in the memory of the Church, as the "Year of Three Popes": Pope Paul VI died on 6 August after a fifteen-year pontificate that had guided the Church through the Second Vatican Council's implementation; his successor, John Paul I, elected in late August, died suddenly after only thirty-three days as pope, plunging the College of Cardinals into a second conclave within the same year, convened in October.

flags.heading: A Surprising Choice
flags.text: On 16 October 1978, the assembled cardinals elected Karol Wojtyła, Archbishop of Kraków, Poland — the first non-Italian pope in 455 years, since the Dutch pope Adrian VI in 1522, and the first Polish pope in the Church's entire history.

flags.heading: A Surprising Choice
flags.text: Wojtyła took the name John Paul II in honor of his immediate predecessor, and appeared on the loggia of St. Peter's Basilica to greet a crowd genuinely startled by the choice of a pope from behind the Iron Curtain.

flags.heading: A Pope Formed by Occupation and Communism
flags.text: Wojtyła's own life had been shaped by decades of totalitarian rule: he had studied for the priesthood in a clandestine underground seminary during the Nazi occupation of Poland, and had spent the whole of his subsequent priestly and episcopal ministry navigating the constraints of a Communist government openly hostile to religious practice — formative experience that gave him, from the very outset of his pontificate, an unusually direct, personally tested understanding of the totalitarian systems then still dividing Europe.

flags.heading: A Pope Formed by Occupation and Communism
flags.text: Wojtyła's own father, a former army officer, raised him largely alone after the early deaths of his mother and only sister, and the future pope lost his elder brother, a physician, to scarlet fever when Karol was still a young man — a series of personal losses that friends and biographers have long connected to the depth of his later pastoral sensitivity to grief and suffering.

flags.heading: "Be Not Afraid"
flags.text: In his inaugural homily on 22 October 1978, John Paul II addressed the whole Church, and the wider world, with words that would define the spirit of his pontificate: "Be not afraid!

flags.heading: "Be Not Afraid"
flags.text: His first pilgrimage to his native Poland the following year, in 1979, drew crowds of millions despite the discouragement of the Communist authorities, and historians widely credit the visit with galvanizing the Solidarity movement that would, within a decade, help bring down Communist rule across Eastern Europe.

flags.heading: Legacy
flags.text: John Paul II went on to lead the Church for over twenty-six years, the third-longest pontificate in history, becoming the most-traveled pope ever, canonizing more saints than all his predecessors combined, and surviving an assassination attempt in 1981 whose perpetrator he personally visited and forgave in prison.

flags.heading: Legacy
flags.text: Canonized himself in 2014, John Paul II remains, for many, simply "John Paul the Great" — a pope whose election out of the very Communist world he would help to dismantle stands as one of the most consequential in the modern history of the papacy.

flags.heading: A Council Calls for a New Catechism
flags.text: The idea of a new, universal catechism for the whole Catholic Church emerged from the Extraordinary Synod of Bishops convened by Pope John Paul II in 1985 to mark the twentieth anniversary of the close of the Second Vatican Council; the assembled bishops, reflecting on two decades of the Council's implementation, called for a single authoritative compendium of Catholic doctrine that could serve as a reliable reference point for the many national and diocesan catechisms then in use across the world.

flags.heading: Six Years of Drafting
flags.text: John Paul II entrusted the project to a commission of twelve cardinals and bishops chaired by Cardinal Joseph Ratzinger, Prefect of the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith, who oversaw an extensive drafting and consultation process that incorporated feedback from bishops' conferences around the world across multiple successive drafts — a genuinely global undertaking intended to produce a text reflecting the Church's teaching with both doctrinal precision and pastoral clarity.

flags.heading: The First Universal Catechism Since Trent
flags.text: John Paul II promulgated the Catechism of the Catholic Church on 11 October 1992, the thirtieth anniversary of the opening of the Second Vatican Council, describing it as a compendium intended to serve bishops and all the Christian faithful as a sure and authentic reference text for teaching Catholic doctrine — the first new universal catechism the Church had produced since the Roman Catechism commissioned by the Council of Trent over four centuries earlier.

flags.heading: Structured Around Four Pillars
flags.text: The new Catechism organized the whole of Catholic teaching around four traditional pillars: the Creed (what the Church believes), the sacraments (how the Church worships and celebrates the mysteries of faith), the moral life (how the Church calls believers to live, organized around the Ten Commandments), and prayer (how the Church prays, organized around the Lord's Prayer) — a structure drawn directly from the pattern of the earlier Roman Catechism, adapted to address the doctrinal and pastoral questions of the contemporary Church.

flags.heading: Legacy
flags.text: A definitive Latin typical edition followed in 1997, correcting and refining the text of the original vernacular editions, and the Catechism has since been translated into dozens of languages, becoming a standard reference for bishops, catechists, and ordinary believers seeking an authoritative and accessible account of Catholic teaching.

flags.heading: Legacy
flags.text: Pope John Paul II himself described the work as a genuine gift to the whole Church, offering, three decades after Vatican II, a single reliable compendium capable of guiding the Council's continued reception into the life of ordinary Catholic belief and practice.

flags.heading: An Announcement in Latin
flags.text: On 11 February 2013, Pope Benedict XVI announced, in Latin, before a small consistory of cardinals gathered for an unrelated matter, that he would resign the papacy effective 28 February — a declaration so unexpected that several of the cardinals present did not immediately grasp its meaning, and one that made Benedict the first pope to resign the office in nearly six hundred years, since Gregory XII's resignation in 1415 had helped end the Western Schism.

flags.heading: An Announcement in Latin
flags.text: Benedict's announcement came at the end of a pontificate of nearly eight years that had followed the long reign of John Paul II, whom Benedict, as Cardinal Joseph Ratzinger, had served for over two decades as Prefect of the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith before his own election in 2005.

flags.heading: A Body No Longer Equal to the Task
flags.text: Benedict explained his decision plainly, citing his advanced age — he was eighty-five — and a declining strength of mind and body that he judged no longer adequate to the demands of the papal office in the modern world, a candor about the physical limits of the papacy itself that had few real precedents in the office's long history.

flags.heading: A Conclave in March
flags.text: The College of Cardinals convened a conclave in Rome in early March 2013, and on 13 March, after just five ballots across two days, elected Cardinal Jorge Mario Bergoglio, Archbishop of Buenos Aires, Argentina — the first pope from the Americas in the Church's entire history, and the first member of the Society of Jesus ever elected to the papacy.

flags.heading: A Name Never Before Chosen
flags.text: Bergoglio took the name Francis, a name no previous pope had ever chosen, in deliberate honor of St. Francis of Assisi and the saint's example of poverty, simplicity, and care for creation — a choice he explained had come to him almost spontaneously in the moment of his election, when a fellow cardinal embraced him and whispered, "Don't forget the poor."

flags.heading: Legacy
flags.text: The near-simultaneous resignation of one pope and election of another, without the intervening death that had marked every previous papal transition for six centuries, raised genuinely new questions about the Church's governance that the papacy had not had to address in the modern era — questions Benedict's own careful conduct as Pope Emeritus, remaining largely withdrawn from public affairs and consistently deferential to his successor, did much to answer through simple, deliberate example rather than any new formal precedent.

flags.heading: Legacy
flags.text: Francis went on to lead the Church for twelve years, until his own death in April 2025, remembered for a pastoral style and set of priorities — mercy, the environment, migrants, and the peripheries of both Church and society — that marked a distinctive chapter in the modern papacy.

flags.heading: The Death of Pope Francis
flags.text: Pope Francis died in Vatican City on 21 April 2025, Easter Monday, after a twelve-year pontificate marked by his emphasis on mercy, care for the environment, and attention to the peripheries of both Church and society; his death, coming only a day after he had made a final public appearance to bless the crowds gathered in St. Peter's Square for Easter, opened a conclave that would draw international attention to an unusually prominent candidate few had expected to see seriously considered only years before.

flags.heading: A Missionary from Chicago
flags.text: Cardinal Robert Francis Prevost, born in Chicago on 14 September 1955 to a family of French, Italian, and Spanish descent, entered the Augustinian order in 1977 and was ordained a priest in 1982.

flags.heading: A Missionary from Chicago
flags.text: He spent much of his priestly ministry as a missionary in Peru, where he later served as Bishop of Chiclayo, and became a naturalized Peruvian citizen in 2015 — a genuinely dual formation, American by birth and Latin American by decades of pastoral service, that shaped his own approach to Church governance.

flags.heading: A Missionary from Chicago
flags.text: Before his appointment to Chiclayo, Prevost had already spent two terms as Prior General of the Augustinian order, from 2001 to 2013, giving him substantial experience in religious governance across the order's many provinces worldwide well before Francis called him to Rome.

flags.heading: Prefect of the Dicastery for Bishops
flags.text: In January 2023, Pope Francis brought Prevost to Rome to serve as Prefect of the Dicastery for Bishops, one of the most consequential offices in the Roman Curia, responsible for vetting episcopal nominations across the entire world, and created him a cardinal later that same year — a position that gave Prevost an unusually broad, direct familiarity with the Church's global episcopate heading into the conclave that would follow Francis's death barely two years later.

flags.heading: The First American Pope
flags.text: The conclave convened in early May 2025, and on 8 May, on its second day of voting, the assembled cardinals elected Prevost as the 267th successor of St. Peter — the first pope in the Church's two-thousand-year history to hold United States citizenship, though his years of ministry and citizenship in Peru meant the election was received, in much of Latin America, as a continuation of the Church's turn toward the Americas that Francis's own election in 2013 had begun.

flags.heading: Taking the Name Leo XIV
flags.text: Prevost took the name Leo XIV, a choice widely understood as a deliberate homage to Pope Leo XIII, the great nineteenth-century pope of Rerum Novarum and the founding document of modern Catholic social teaching — a signal, many commentators suggested, of the new pope's own priorities regarding labor, human dignity, and the Church's engagement with a rapidly changing economic and technological world.

flags.heading: Legacy
flags.text: In the opening period of his pontificate, Leo XIV addressed issues including the rights of migrants, environmental protection, the rise of artificial intelligence, and continued divisions within the Church between more traditional and more progressive currents, in ways many observers read as continuous with the priorities of his predecessor while carrying his own distinct emphasis and voice.
